title: Carbon Trading Opportunity and Challenges in Ethiopia
content:
International carbon offsets and global carbon markets were created to direct carbon financing for the mitigation of climate change toward emerging and impoverished nations. Companies, governments, and people purchased approximately 1 billion carbon offsets in the voluntary carbon markets during the past ten years, contributing slightly under $4.5 billion to clean energy and conservation. This review study aims to evaluate the extent of carbon trading, opportunities and challenges associated with carbon trading in Ethiopia, and potential solutions for issues linked to the concerns presented. Compared to several Asian and Western countries, very few carbon emissions come from African nations. 
Buyers and sellers exchange "carbon offsets" or "carbon credits," which are measurements of carbon emissions that have been cut at the source, in carbon markets. Project based transactions and trade in emission allowances are the two main categories of transactions that make up these marketplaces. A local carbon emissions trading scheme in East Africa/Ethiopia might produce trading volumes, foster transparency, support local investment projects, and make the system more adaptable. There exist certain obstacles to carbon trading in East Africa; the two main ones being the unpredictability of the potential benefits and the high transaction costs. 
The money made from the sale of carbon should be distributed across the nations, especially those with the guts and the desire to preserve forest resources. East African countries' ability to implement projects must be strengthened by offering various chances for skill development. 
Ethiopia won't be able to cut its carbon emissions without carbon markets. The nation must develop a coherent plan on gas emission factors by determining environmentally suitable substitutes, like modern, sustainable agriculture and renewable energy sources. This is particularly significant for industries like agriculture, the production of charcoal from native plants, and the burning of wood for fuel.
